title: Building Blocks: From Words to Sentences
brief: Introduce the word-to-sentence progression using the Word Bricks framework from the source. Explain how beginning-level students construct short phrases or simple sentences while intermediate and advanced students build longer ones, and how special bricks (-s, Wild Card, -ed, -ing, -ly) allow students to create alternate word forms. Describe the teacher's role in demonstrating that Word Bricks contain words on either side and how adjusting the number of Wild Cards changes the difficulty level. Connect this physical manipulation of words to the cognitive process of understanding how sentences are assembled from individual parts of speech.

title: Controlled Writing: Sentence Patterns and Boundaries
brief: Explain controlled writing as a scaffold in which the teacher sets precise constraints on what students produce, drawing on the Sentence Boundaries game from the source. Detail how patterns such as 'exactly 5 words,' 'exactly 8 words,' '1 sentence with 2 verbs,' or '1 sentence with 1 adjective and 1 adverb' give learners a clear, bounded target. Describe how the teacher evaluates grammatical correctness and, when a sentence is incorrect, returns responsibility to the team to keep revising rather than correcting for them. Frame these constraints as practical scaffolds that move students from open-ended production toward accurate, purposeful sentence construction.

title: Guided Writing: Sentence Frames and Word Charts
brief: Introduce guided writing as a middle stage between controlled and free production, drawing on the word-chart and sentence-frame approach described in the source's rainforest lesson. Explain how organizing vocabulary by part of speech (adjectives, nouns, verbs, adverbs, prepositions/adverbs of place) in visible columns allows students to string together a wide variety of sentences while still following a model. Describe how the teacher uses color-coded ink for each part of speech and asks students to read aloud, sing, and act out sentences before writing their own. Show how students then produce individually—writing three sentences in their journals following the practiced model—as the natural endpoint of guided practice.

title: The Topic Sentence: Anchor of the Paragraph
brief: Define the topic sentence as the organizing anchor of a paragraph, drawing on the source's Self-Editing and Peer Editing Checklist station on topic sentences, which asks whether topic sentences use language similar to that in the thesis statement. Explain the relationship between a topic sentence and the explaining sentences that follow it, which the source describes as sentences that add more information about the main idea. Introduce the concept of evidence sentences (specific examples to support the main idea) and interpreting sentences (sentences that tell the reader the importance or meaning of the evidence and explain why it supports the topic sentence). Present these four sentence types—topic, explaining, evidence, interpreting—as the practical building blocks of a basic paragraph.

title: Basic Paragraph Organization: From Opening to Closing
brief: Walk through the internal structure of a complete paragraph using the station checklist from the source as the organizing framework. Cover the closing sentence, which the source defines as restating the main point, and explain how it gives the paragraph a sense of completion. Introduce the concept of bridges—clauses or phrases that review the previous paragraph and/or preview the following one—as a tool for connecting paragraphs once students move beyond a single paragraph. Describe how a teacher can use the station-based checklist approach at a simplified level (a single paragraph or even just a couple of sentences for beginning students) so that the organizational framework scales to the class level.

title: Peer Feedback as a Writing Scaffold
brief: Present peer feedback not as an assessment tool but as a practical scaffold that keeps writing active and iterative, drawing on the self-editing and peer-editing activity described in the source. Explain the station-based process: students highlight one part of their writing at each station, reach agreement with a classmate, and initial the checklist before moving on, working with several different peers to get a range of feedback. Note the source's observation that when students notice another student's essay is missing a component, they go back and double-check their own writing as well, making the process mutually reinforcing. Acknowledge the source's identified challenges (less teacher control, time-consuming setup) alongside the benefits (students feel more in control, do not see the teacher as the only authority), and note that the teacher still provides feedback alongside student feedback.
